The **2004 presidential campaign of John Edwards**, then a U.S. senator from [North Carolina], formally began on September 16, 2003, when he announced his candidacy for the [Democratic presidential nomination] in [Robbins, North Carolina].[[2]][[3]] Edwards emerged as a major challenger to [John Kerry], particularly after a second-place finish in the [Iowa caucuses], and he generally avoided direct attacks on his Democratic rivals for much of the campaign.[[4]][[5]] Near the end of the primary campaign, he more sharply characterized Kerry as a "[Washington insider]", particularly over [trade policy].[[6]][[7]]

After Kerry won nine of the ten states holding contests on [Super Tuesday], Edwards formally withdrew on March 3, 2004, and endorsed Kerry.[[8]][[9]] Kerry announced on July 6 that Edwards would be his running mate and the Democratic vice-presidential nominee.[[10]] The [Kerry-Edwards] ticket lost the November general election to incumbent [Republican] "Republican Party (United States)")[president][George W. Bush] and [Vice President][Dick Cheney].[[11]]

## Background and announcement

[[edit]]

[![Image 5]]

John Edwards campaigning in [New Hampshire], January 25th 2004

In 2000, Edwards unofficially began laying the groundwork for a possible presidential campaign by seeking speaking engagements and political contacts in early nominating states, including [Iowa]. His eventual campaign chairman, North Carolina Democratic activist [Ed Turlington], had begun introducing Edwards to influential Democrats in early states before the 2000 presidential election.[[12]] On January 2, 2003, Edwards formed a presidential exploratory committee, allowing him to begin raising money for a possible candidacy.[[13]][[14]] On September 15, 2003, Edwards announced his intention to seek the nomination during an appearance on _[The Daily Show with Jon Stewart]_, fulfilling an earlier promise that he would tell Stewart first if he decided to run.[[15]][[16]] He formally launched the campaign the following morning in [Robbins], the [North Carolina] town where he had grown up, speaking near the textile mill where his father had worked.[[17]][[18]]

At the launch, Edwards emphasized economic opportunity and his [working-class] family background, arguing that the [Bush administration] had favored powerful interests over ordinary workers and the [middle class].[[19]][[20]] A week before his formal launch, Edwards had announced that he would not seek reelection to the Senate in 2004, saying that he would concentrate on the presidential campaign.[[21]][[22]] Turlington served as chairman of the campaign.[[23]]

## Campaign timeline

[[edit]]

### Early campaign

[[edit]]

[![Image 6]].jpg)

John Edwards speaking at [Nashua], [New Hampshire], November 7th 2003

As Edwards had been building support well before formally announcing his candidacy, he led the Democratic field in initial campaign fundraising. His committee reported about $7.4 million in receipts during the first quarter of 2003.[[24]][[25]] More than half of the money came from people associated with the legal profession, reflecting Edwards' previous career as a trial lawyer and his extensive network among plaintiffs' attorneys.[[26]][[27]]

Edwards' stump speech centered on the theme of "two Americas", contrasting the [economic] and political opportunities available to [wealthy] and [powerful Americans] with those available to [working] and [middle-class] families.[[28]][[29]] The theme, together with Edwards' emphasis on fairness, jobs and economic opportunity, led news coverage to characterize his campaign as a form of southern or [economic populism].[[30]] Edwards also made his refusal to engage in sustained personal attacks on Democratic opponents part of his campaign style, describing his message as positive and "uplifting".[[31]][[32]]

### First nominating contests

[[edit]]

Edwards struggled to gain substantial support for much of 2003, but his poll numbers rose sharply in the final weeks before the [Iowa caucuses]. As recently as November he had been polling in single digits there, and his late momentum was aided by the endorsement of _[The Des Moines Register]_ and growing crowds at campaign events.[[33]] Edwards finished a surprising second in Iowa with 32 percent of state delegate equivalents, behind Kerry's 38 percent and ahead of former front-runner [Howard Dean] at 18 percent.[[34]][[35]] One week later in the [New Hampshire primary], he finished fourth behind Kerry, Dean and [Wesley Clark], with about 12 percent of the vote.[[36]][[37]]

During the February 3 contests, Edwards won the [South Carolina] primary with about 45 percent of the vote, his first statewide victory.[[38]][[39]] In [Oklahoma], he finished narrowly behind Clark, while Kerry won [Arizona], [Delaware], [Missouri], [New Mexico] and [North Dakota].[[40]][[41]] Kerry then won the February 7 caucuses in [Michigan] and [Washington]; Edwards finished third in Michigan and fourth in Washington, having focused more heavily on the approaching contests in the [South].[[42]][[43]]

Edwards subsequently finished second to Kerry in [Tennessee] and [Virginia]. In [Wisconsin] on February 17, he again finished second, receiving about 34 percent to Kerry's 40 percent and Dean's 18 percent.[[44]][[45]] Dean ended his active campaign the following day, leaving Edwards as Kerry's only remaining major challenger and turning the contest into a two-man race ahead of the ten-state March 2 round.[[46]][[47]]
